activities.anchor: A grayscale image is a 2-D array
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the pixel soup
activities.name: cnxPixelsEstimate

config.prompt: A 224 × 224 colour photo carries three channels of brightness values. Roughly how many numbers is that?
config.why: 224 × 224 × 3 ≈ 150,000 values — the raw pixel soup the CNN must turn into concepts like 'pedestrian'.
config.context: A convolutional layer of 64 different 3×3 filters over 3 channels needs just 64 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 1,728 weights to start that translation.

activities.anchor: Why slide one small kernel instead of connecting every pixel to every neuron?
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the parameter-count argument
activities.name: cnxWeightsSpot

config.prompt: This architecture argument contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Images are local: pixel neighbourhoods are where structure lives.
A fully-connected hidden layer of 1,000 units over 224×224×3 needs about 150 million weights.
64 different 3×3 filters over 3 channels need 64 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 1,728 weights — four orders of magnitude fewer.
Padding adds a border so the output map stays the same size; stride skips positions to shrink it.
Weight sharing is a compromise: connecting every pixel to every neuron uses more information, so it recognises more.
config.correction: Fully-connected uses more parameters, not more information — and throws away locality; weight sharing encodes the prior that the same pattern matters wherever it appears.
config.why: That is how 1,728 weights can beat 150 million on real images — cheaper to train, harder to overfit, and structurally committed to the right prior.

activities.caption: which curve is the receptive field?
activities.name: cnxFieldTrace

config.prompt: Each layer takes a 3×3 view of the previous layer's larger features, so the effective view compounds. Which curve matches a neuron's effective receptive field (in pixels) as layers (x) stack?
config.why: The compounding view is depth's whole trick: a neuron at layer 5 can 'see' a quarter of the picture — edges into textures into parts into objects, self-organised.

activities.caption: rebuild the lineage — cortex to cheque digits
activities.name: cnxLineageOrder

config.prompt: The biological echo became an architecture — put the lineage in order:
items: Hubel and Wiesel find simple and complex cells in cat visual cortex (1959–62)
Fukushima's neocognitron translates the circuit idea into a layered network (1980)
LeCun's LeNet adds backpropagation and reads bank cheque digits (1989–98)
Zeiler & Fergus visualise trained networks — the hierarchy was there, self-organised (2014)
config.why: The architecture only says 'local filters, shared, stacked'; the specific features emerge from training — visualisation confirmed what was learned, not designed.

activities.caption: pin the human on the top-5 error scale
activities.name: cnxHumanPlace

config.prompt: AlexNet cut top-5 error to 15.3% in 2012; ResNet reached 3.6% by 2015. Where does a careful HUMAN sit on the same task?
config.why: About 5% — by 2015 residual networks had pushed machine top-5 error below the careful human's roughly 5%, which is why 2012 is called the ImageNet moment: deep learning became the default method.
config.context: The runner-up scored 26.2% the year AlexNet's two gaming GPUs, ReLUs and dropout dropped eleven points in one go.

activities.anchor: the network "sees" the way you do
activities.caption: true or false — machine vision's way of seeing
activities.name: cnxSeesJudge

statements.s: CNNs lean heavily on texture and local statistics where humans use shape and context.
statements.why: Visualisation experiments suggest the mismatch — the networks solve the task with features that are statistically effective, not human-like.

statements.s: The network 'sees' the way you do.
statements.why: It leans on texture and local statistics; models confidently misclassify objects photographed in unusual poses.

statements.s: A lesioned texture can fool human and machine in opposite ways.
statements.why: One image, two opposite errors — the clearest demonstration that the feature sets differ.

statements.s: CNN features are designed layer by layer by engineers.
statements.why: Nobody specifies the hierarchy — it emerges from training on labelled images; visualisation studies confirmed it afterwards.

activities.caption: pair each vision task with its output
activities.name: cnxTaskMatch

config.prompt: From classification down to pixels — pair each task with what it delivers:

pairs.right: bounding boxes for many objects in one forward pass — fast enough for video
a label for every pixel — the boundary of the tumour, not just 'tumour somewhere'
superhuman consistency in narrow tasks, superhuman fragility outside them

config.why: Detection makes self-driving perception and photo search possible; segmentation is medical imaging's workhorse.

activities.anchor: Three stand out, and each has changed practice
activities.caption: file the failure — which classic is it?
activities.name: cnxFailBuckets

config.prompt: Three classic failure modes — file each case:

items.label: an invisible perturbation flips the panda to 'gibbon' with high confidence (2017)
road signs are fair game for adversaries too
a 'skin lesion classifier' that learned ruler marks from malignant-photo datasets
a 'sheep detector' that keyed on grass
one hospital's scanners lose accuracy on another's

config.why: If the training data contains a shortcut, the optimiser will take it — and a broken model fails silently, so the professional response is one discipline: evaluate on data that looks like the real world, test failure cases on purpose, monitor after launch.
